answer: Wind gusts rise and fall in an envelope that two microphones a few metres apart will share almost exactly, so a device can prove co-location by correlating the gust envelope of its recording with a neighbour's recording over the same minute. The envelope is driven by live weather and cannot be predicted, and a farm would need a separate windy microphone for every claimed outdoor location. A prism of separate recordings splits one gust into agreeing shapes, a sable of dark clouds brings the next gust, and the mesa of flat ground lets the wind arrive at both microphones together or not at all.
